 Tucker Carlson: Demon Hunter 
 Demons and the supernatural mentioned at least 644 times on Tucker Carlson’s show
 Written by Gideon Taaffe , Noah VanDowe & Hanne MacDonald 
 Research contributions from Kayla Gogarty & Jack Wheatley 
 Published 
 10/31/26 1:54 AM EDT 
 Nearly a quarter of episodes of Tucker Carlson’s online show feature claims about demons, alleged occult activity, and/or the supernatural, including discussions of “ritual killing” and people suffering from “demonic possession.” Supernatural themes have increased dramatically on Carlson’s show as he has  reinvented himself as an independent power center on the right,  vowing to “help build a third party,” releasing his 10-point vision for America, and fueling speculation about a potential third-party run.
 Select a section
 Carlson and his guests have mentioned demons or the supernatural at least 644 times on Carlson’s show, and the volume of mentions has increased each year 
 Carlson is pushing his obsession with demons and the supernatural to massive audiences 
 Guests on Carlson's show, including an exorcist, described interactions with demons 
 Since leaving Fox, Carlson has become a divisive figure in right-wing media, rebranding in part by infusing politics with talk of demons 
 Methodology 
 A “ kingmaker in the Republican Party ” before he was fired by Fox, Carlson has attempted to rebuild his influence within conservative politics and media in the years since, increasingly pandering to  far-right Christian and   antisemitic corners by interweaving talk of demons and politics. This includes suggesting his opponents are  subject to “ demonic influence ” and that “ the leadership of the world ” is “becoming just sort of openly demonic.”
 Carlson, who is  reportedly toying with the idea of launching a new political party, has a massive online audience, with at least 21.3 million subscribers and followers across streaming and social media platforms. His YouTube channel alone has amassed 555 million views so far this year. 
 Media Matters reviewed episodes of  The Tucker Carlson Show on YouTube from the show's  launch in December 2023 through the end of July 2026, finding hundreds of mentions of demons and the supernatural from Carlson and his guests — with substantial increases in mentions each year. 
 Key findings:
 Nearly 1 in 4 episodes of  The Tucker Carlson Show have included mentions of demons and/or the supernatural.
 Together these episodes (nearly a quarter of all episodes) included at least 644 mentions of demons and the supernatural and collectively earned over 109 million views on YouTube.
 Mentions of demons and the supernatural have increased considerably year after year. From 2024 to 2025, mentions increased by 313% . The first seven months of 2026 have already seen a 55% increase over all of 2025.
 Since being  ousted from Fox News in April 2023, Carlson has repeatedly discussed demons in interviews both on and off his  own streaming network , which  includes   The Tucker Carlson Show . During a 2024 interview for the documentary  Christianities? , for example, Carlson  claimed he was “attacked” and “physically mauled” by a demon in his sleep. The Wall Street Journal’s Bojan Pancevski also  reported an “extraordinary five-hour discussion” in which Carlson described, among other things, his “belief in aliens as manifestations of demons and angels.” 
 Carlson and his guests have mentioned demons or the supernatural at least 644 times on Carlson’s show, and the volume of mentions has increased each year 
 Media Matters reviewed YouTube transcripts of all 303 episodes of  The Tucker Carlson Show  that were listed on the show's YouTube  playlist through the end of July 2026, identifying mentions of the words demon, demonic, or supernatural, as well as variations. 
 Based on this review, we found 644 mentions in 75 episodes. These 75 episodes, which accounted for roughly a quarter of all episodes, earned over 109 million views on YouTube. 
 We also found substantial increases in mentions each year. Between 2024 and 2025, mentions increased 313%, with 56 mentions in 2024 and 231 mentions in 2025. In the first seven months of 2026, we found 357 mentions, representing a 55% increase over the total for all of 2025.
 Carlson is pushing his obsession with demons and the supernatural to massive audiences 
 Carlson has more than 21.3 million subscribers and followers on streaming and social media platforms — including  YouTube ,  Rumble ,  Facebook ,  Instagram , and  TikTok  — where he streams his show and/or posts clips from it. Based on data collected from SocialBlade, Carlson has amassed over 2.4 million new subscribers and followers on these platforms in 2026 alone, with his  YouTube   channel earning over 555 million views and his TikTok content earning at least 28.4 million  likes .
 Media Matters’ review of  The Tucker Carlson Show also found that roughly 28% of mentions of variations of demon, demonic, or supernatural came from Carlson himself.

 Below is just a sampling of the kinds of comments Carlson is pushing to his massive audiences on  The Tucker Carlson Show : 
 Carlson referred to abortion as a form of “ritual killing” through which people “derive power,” including potential “demonic power.” Carlson: “There's no question in my mind that … the ritual killing of other people, whether through war, abortion, or euthanasia, the death penalty — it's a religious ritual. … And through killing, the shedding of blood of others, especially of innocents, they derive power.” [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show ,  4/17/26 ]
 Carlson claimed “powerful people” are “the most religious people of all,” adding, “They’re just not worshipping the same god. … They believe they're special because they're getting supernatural power, and I think it's demonic power.” Carlson: “I have been around powerful people for so long that one thing I've learned is they're the most religious people of all. And they all pretend to be agnostic or, I don't believe in anything, I believe in science. No, no, no, no, no. They are observant religious people. They're just not worshiping the same god. But they think their power is supernatural. There's no doubt about it. I know them, and they believe they're special because they're getting supernatural power, and I think it's demonic power. I think it's really obvious.” [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show , 4/17/26 ]
 Carlson has repeatedly suggested that nuclear weapons are “inspired by supernatural forces” and “demonically inspired.” In a 2025 conversation with Columbia University’s Ivana Hughes, Carlson said, “I think nuclear weapons are evil, I think they're actually probably inspired by supernatural forces, that's my view, and I think they've wrecked the world already.” He also told priest Chad Ripperger in 2026, “You look at something like AI or nuclear weapons, specifically — hard not to think that that was demonically inspired.” [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show , 10/17/25 , 4/3/26 ]
 Carlson said, “There's a reason that people worship demons, not just because they're inherently perverse, but because it works short term.” Carlson also said, “That’s why … the Incas sacrificed children, so did the Mayans and the Aztecs and the Vikings and like — when you sacrifice a virgin to the rain god, it actually rains.” The episode was titled “Jay Dyer: Demons in Hollywood, CIA, Secret Societies, Lone Gunmen, Epstein & Attacks on Christianity.” [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show , 7/13/26, 7/13/26 ]
 Carlson also claimed that “the leadership of the world” is “becoming just sort of openly demonic.” The world is “moving in a way that's just more explicitly evil,” he said. [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show , 5/29/26 ]
 Carlson has called things like the internet, AI, and rock and roll demonic.  He declared, “I do think the internet's demonic,” and said that working on the internet “makes me uncomfortable.” While discussing rock and roll in another episode, Carlson said, “Of course it's demonic.” He also claimed that it's “hard not to think” AI “was demonically inspired,” and while discussing AI and transhumanism, he alleged that “creepy billionaires in the tech world” are “being controlled by spiritual forces, by demons.” [YouTube,  The Tucker Carlson Show , 10/13/25 , 10/3/25 , 4/3/26 , 10/3/24 ]
 Guests on Carlson's show, including an exorcist, described interactions with demons 
 Roughly 72% of all mentions of demons or the supernatural came from Carlson’s guests, who have ranged from fellow political pundits — including Mike Cernovich , Jack Posobiec , and Alex Jones — to religious figures and writers. Religious figures have included  Chad Ripperger , an  exorcist ; Christian  author   Lee Strobel ;  Rev.   Stephen De Young ;  filmmaker   Sean Stone and  writer Conrad Flynn have also joined.
 In his episode with Carlson titled “Exorcist Fr. Chad Ripperger: Possessed Politicians, Occult Activity, and Speaking to Satan Himself,” Ripperger claimed there exists a “council” of five demons who “execute the plans of Satan,” including Asmodeus, the “demon of homosexuality in men.” Ripperger explained, “If you have a guy that is possessed and he’s had homosexual experience, it’s a pretty good bet that Asmodeus is one of the possessors.” [YouTube,  The Tucker Carlson Show , 4/3/26 , 4/3/26 ]
 Ripperger further argued that abortion exists in the United States because “the demons empower the people that are keeping it in place because they, the demons, love abortion, basically.” [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show , 4/3/26 ]
 In another episode titled “Ex-Freemason: Possessed Politicians, Demonic Rituals for Power, Secret Societies, and the Occult,” Carlson listened credulously as Sean Stone claimed to have received a direct phone call from “Azazel,” whom he described as “the angel of death.” When Carlson pressed as to what the “angel of death” told him, Stone responded that he didn't “remember specifically an announcement of something,” but that he was getting “so many calls” from “things wanting my soul.” [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show , 5/18/26 , 5/18/26 ]
 Conspiracy theorist Alex Jones told Carlson that people will have to “choose a side,” describing one side as the “satanic world order,” and claimed there is a pattern of women becoming “demon-possessed.” Carlson agreed that “what you just described is just on display everywhere,” suggesting leftists are “worshipping death in some way.” [YouTube, The Tucker Carlson Show , 4/9/25 ]
 Since leaving Fox, Carlson has become a divisive figure in right-wing media, rebranding in part by infusing politics with talk of demons 
 Carlson and President Donald Trump’s relationship has broken down in public over the last year, with the president calling him “low IQ” and Carlson in turn suggesting that the man he once campaigned for could actually be “the antichrist.”
 As tension mounts between Carlson and the right-wing ecosystem , some other figures ostracized by the MAGA movement, including former Trump official Joe Kent and former Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, have reportedly met to discuss their concerns about Trump, the current GOP, and the need for a new political “movement.” Carlson — whose commentary has veered further into religious fundamentalism in recent years — has claimed “It’s Time to Save America” and singled out Trump as “flamboyantly corrupt.”
 On August 5, roughly a month after declaring his intent to “help build a third party,” Carlson released a 10-point “manifesto” laying out qualities he says “America should be,” fueling speculation of a potential third-party presidential run. While Carlson has denied having any intention of running, some of his allies are reportedly actively trying to convince him.
 Carlson's rhetoric is consistent with a trend among some in right-wing media of infusing and ramping up apocalyptic political rhetoric that stems in part from a growing Christian nationalist movement. This rhetoric demonizes LGBTQ people, perceived political enemies, and progressive causes, including by deploying rhetoric about “ demonic ” influence and an existential , “ spiritual” war. Already, purported evil spirits, demons, and satanic influences have served as the foundation to several wild ideas in right-wing media relating to the Biden administration , Trump's legal troubles , aliens , television , artificial intelligence , the 2024 Super Bowl , and popular musicians such as Cardi B, Beyoncé, and Ariana Grande. And this rhetoric is being disseminated to large audiences who have become increasingly reliant on an ecosystem of podcasts and online shows (overwhelmingly dominated by those that are right-leaning ) for their news.
 Even some of Carlson’s critics see his talk of demons as no laughing matter. On The Jeremy Boreing Show, conservative writer Rod Dreher revealed that he “connected [Carlson] with an exorcist I know” following the former Fox host’s claim that he was attacked by a demon. Dreher explained, “I do believe absolutely in spiritual warfare, and the exorcists I've talked to who know about his case are incredibly worried about him. They say he's in deep, deep danger, and he also has the ear of the vice president of the United States.”
 Methodology 
 Media Matters reviewed all 303 episodes of  The Tucker Carlson Show that were listed on the show's playlist on Carlson's YouTube channel and spanned from the show's launch in December 2023 through July 31, 2026. We excluded 5 episodes that were unavailable or hidden from the playlist and 50 videos in the playlist that were from other shows or appearances.
 For each episode, a researcher searched the YouTube transcript and identified all mentions of the following keywords: “demon,” “demons,” “demonically,” “demonized human,” “demonic,” “demoniac,” “supernatural,” or “supernaturally.” For each mention, researchers also identified the speaker.
 Another researcher independently searched each episode's transcript in the Fight.fudgie.org podcast database for the keywords. We manually reviewed each mention in the database and identified the speaker.
 A third researcher compared the mentions and speakers identified in the YouTube transcripts with those identified in the Fight.fudgie.org podcast database, reconciling any differences.
